# ML-2 extensions: generated by `extend.py`, not hand-edited

## 1. Confidence intervals: the first build had one seed

3 independent training runs (seeds [11, 22, 33]), 95% t-intervals.

| metric | mean ± half-width | sd |
|---|---|---|
| known supervised auroc | 0.877 ± 0.016 | 0.007 |
| known anomaly auroc | 0.843 ± 0.023 | 0.009 |
| unseen supervised auroc | 0.779 ± 0.051 | 0.020 |
| unseen anomaly auroc | 0.956 ± 0.036 | 0.015 |

**The unseen-defect gap is +0.176 ± 0.020.**

The interval excludes zero, so the anomaly head does beat the supervised head on the held-out class, but look at the size. A gap of this magnitude is a real effect and a small one, and the first build's single-seed number could not have told you which.

## 1b. Why the first pass reported 0.958, and why that was luck

The first pass reported unseen-class supervised AUROC **0.958** from one training run, and concluded from it that the unseen-defect experiment had failed: the supervised head scored *higher* on the held-out class than on the classes it was trained on, which is the opposite of the effect the two-stage architecture is supposed to exploit.

The three seeds above land near 0.78, which is nine standard deviations away. Something other than sampling had to be responsible, and there was an obvious candidate: `extend.py` trains on 1100 images for 12 epochs and `run_inspect.py` on 1400 for 14. Two variables had moved at once, so the honest move was to hold the seeds fixed and sweep only the budget (`python budget_probe.py`).

**The budget was not the cause.**

| training budget | known sup | unseen sup | known ano | unseen ano | gap (ano − sup) |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1100 imgs / 12 ep | 0.877 | **0.779** | 0.843 | 0.956 | +0.176 |
| 1400 imgs / 14 ep | 0.888 | **0.740** | 0.863 | 0.951 | +0.210 |

At the first pass's own budget the unseen supervised AUROC averages **0.740** over three seeds, not 0.958, and the spread is the finding: **sd 0.096**, against 0.020 at the smaller budget. 0.958 sits about 2.3 standard deviations above that mean. It was a lucky seed, reported as a result.

### What that does to the first pass's conclusion

**It reverses it.** The anomaly head beats the supervised head on the held-out class in **6 of 6 runs** across both budgets (gaps +0.182, +0.167, +0.180, +0.098, +0.274, +0.259; smallest +0.098). A sign test on 6/6 gives one-sided p = 0.016, which is distribution-free and therefore immune to the variance blow-up that makes the t-interval at the larger budget useless.

And the degradation the first pass went looking for and failed to find is there:

| training budget | supervised: known → unseen | anomaly: known → unseen |
|---|---|---|
| 1100 imgs / 12 ep | 0.877 → 0.779 (**-0.098**) | 0.843 → 0.956 (+0.113) |
| 1400 imgs / 14 ep | 0.888 → 0.740 (**-0.147**) | 0.863 → 0.951 (+0.088) |

The supervised head **loses** AUROC on a defect class it never saw; the anomaly head **gains** it. That is the structural claim the two-stage architecture rests on, and the first pass declared it unsupported on the strength of a single run.

### What I am not claiming

Three seeds per cell. At the larger budget the gap's own 95% interval is +0.210 ± 0.241, which **includes zero**: the variance is large enough that the parametric interval says nothing there. The sign test across all six runs is the claim I will defend; the effect size is not pinned down, and pinning it down means more seeds.

I also have no confirmed mechanism for why the larger budget is so much noisier. The plausible story is that more epochs on three defect classes lets the model commit harder to class-specific features, and how far it commits varies by initialisation, but that is a hypothesis I have not tested, and it is written here as one.

**The transferable lesson is the cheap one.** A single-seed result was strong enough to become this project's headline negative finding, and it was wrong. Nothing about it looked fragile: it was a clean AUROC on a clean holdout. The only thing that would have caught it is the discipline of never reporting a model comparison from one run, which costs three trainings and is the reason section 1 exists at all.

## 2. The two-stage cascade, wired

Stage 1 (anomaly screen) threshold chosen for **99% target recall**: 9.8979. Stage 2 names a class above 0.2926.

| | known defects | unseen defect |
|---|---|---|
| ACCEPT | 31 | 10 |
| FLAG_FOR_REVIEW | 452 | 239 |
| REJECT_CLASSIFIED | 217 | 101 |
| **stage-1 recall** | **98.8%** | **100.0%** |

**The third verdict is the one that matters.** `FLAG_FOR_REVIEW`, stage 1 is confident something is wrong, stage 2 cannot name it, is the disposition an unseen defect should receive. A two-outcome system forces the operator to pick a wrong class to clear the screen, and then the override log fills with garbage and poisons the retraining set.

### The throughput argument

Stage 1 costs 12.11 ms/part, stage 2 8.28 ms. At a line prevalence of 0.5% the screen flags 93.9% of parts, so stage 2 runs on that fraction only:

| | ms per part |
|---|---|
| cascade (stage 1 + 93.9% × stage 2) | **19.89** |
| both stages on every part | 20.39 |
| saving | 2.5% |

**The throughput argument does not survive contact with the measured screen rate.** A cascade saves time only when the cheap stage *clears* most parts, and this screen clears 6.1%. Stage 2 therefore runs on nearly everything and the saving is 2.5%: a rounding error against a takt budget, and nowhere near enough to justify two models, two thresholds and two retraining paths.

The cause is not the cascade, it is the screen. A 99% recall target on an anomaly head whose known-defect AUROC is ~0.84 buys that recall by putting the threshold low enough to flag almost everything, and recall bought that way is real and worthless.

So the conclusion is narrower than the one I set out to write: **this is the right architecture for the wrong model.** `FLAG_FOR_REVIEW` justifies the cascade on its own: an unseen defect needs a disposition that is neither ACCEPT nor a guessed class. The latency saving is a separate claim, and on this model I have not earned it.

Either way the saving depends entirely on the screen rate, which depends on prevalence: the same Bayes arithmetic as the PPV table in RESULTS.md, arriving this time as a latency budget.

#### What the recall target costs, swept

| stage-1 recall target | achieved | good parts flagged | screen rate @0.5% prevalence | cascade ms/part | saving | defects escaping |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 99.9% | 99.6% | 96.1% | 96.1% | 20.06 | 1.6% | 0.4% |
| 99.0% | 98.8% | 93.9% | 93.9% | 19.89 | 2.5% | 1.2% |
| 95.0% | 95.0% | 77.8% | 77.9% | 18.56 | 9.0% | 5.0% |
| 90.0% | 90.0% | 64.9% | 65.1% | 17.50 | 14.2% | 10.0% |
| 80.0% | 80.1% | 41.8% | 42.1% | 15.60 | 23.5% | 19.9% |

This table is the decision surface, and it prices a **safety-vs-cost trade in milliseconds**: every point of recall given up buys throughput and ships defects. The last column is why the saving column cannot be read on its own: the cheap rows are cheap precisely because they let defects through.

Read down it and the shape of the problem is plain. The saving only becomes interesting once the screen is clearing a real fraction of good parts, and on this model that does not happen until the recall target has dropped into a range no inspection engineer would sign. **That is a verdict on the anomaly head, not on the cascade**: the same architecture on a screen with a sharper healthy/defective separation would show this table tilting the other way.

## 3. Grad-CAM: the supervised head had no localisation at all

On 120 defective images, the Grad-CAM peak lands **inside the true defect mask 3.3%** of the time. Defect pixels are 0.80% of image area, so a random peak would land inside about 0.80% of the time.

That is a **4× lift over chance**, which is the comparison that makes the number mean something: a localisation score quoted without the base rate is unreadable, because defects are small and any peak is *usually* outside the mask by area alone.

Grad-CAM is coarse by construction: it is the spatial resolution of the last convolutional layer, upsampled. The spec calls it a *minimum* rather than a substitute for segmentation.

**A 4× lift is not the same as a usable one, and I am not going to let the lift do the talking.** The peak lands outside the true defect 96.7% of the time. An operator shown that overlay is being pointed at the wrong part of the part in roughly nineteen cases out of twenty, and a localisation aid that is usually wrong is worse than none: it teaches the operator to distrust the overlay, and then to distrust the call the overlay arrived with.

The diagnosis is in the training objective rather than in Grad-CAM. The head is trained on an image-level label, so it is free to key on anything that correlates with the label anywhere in the frame, and the first build already caught this model doing exactly that, when global average pooling washed the defects out. **An attribution method cannot manufacture spatial evidence the model never used.** Raising this number is a segmentation or patch-supervision job, which is named in the not-built list, and it is not a Grad-CAM tuning exercise.

## 4. The operator override log

1009 parts reached the review station.

| disposition | count |
|---|---|
| CONFIRMED_DEFECT | 267 |
| FALSE_REJECT | 597 |
| UNCLASSIFIED | 145 |

**Operator-confirmed PPV: 0.309.** This is the only PPV measurable in production without a destructive audit, and it is measured on the *flagged subset*, not on the line, so it is an upper bound on line PPV rather than an estimate of it. Confusing the two is how a monitoring dashboard reports healthy precision on a line that is scrapping good parts.

Defects that escaped stage 1 entirely: 3 known, 0 unseen. Those never reach a human, which is why stage 1 is tuned for recall and why its threshold is the one number in this system worth arguing about.

**Why the log is retraining gold, and why it is also a trap.** It is gold because of the *sampling*: these are labels on exactly the parts the model found hard, which is the most informative set to buy. It is a trap for the same reason: it is a censored sample, containing only what stage 1 flagged, so a model retrained on it alone drifts toward the screen's own biases and gets worse on the parts nobody ever reviewed.

**The operator is simulated as ground truth here, which is generous.** A real operator is a measurement system with its own repeatability and reproducibility, which is precisely the spec's gauge-R&R question, and it remains unbuilt.
